About the Physician Assistant - Medical Case Challenge event

Physician Assistant - Medical Case Challenge is a Health Professions event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing · speech & presentation.

Ten in-depth lessons for the new HOSA Physician Assistant – Medical Case Challenge (2026–27): the full test plan (diagnosis 14%, patient assessment 12%, disease process and cancer 10%, and every body system from circulatory and digestive at 10% to integumentary, reproductive and urinary at 4%) and the Round Two case review and five-minute team presentation. Built around CMDT and MedlinePlus, with history-taking and diagnostic-reasoning drills, labeled body-system diagrams, lab-pattern matching, an ECG rhythm lab, case scenarios in every lesson and a full practice case. Always base your presentation on the case documents you are given.

Sample Physician Assistant - Medical Case Challenge questions

1. In the abdominal exam, why is auscultation done before palpation?

  1. Auscultation is the most important step
  2. Palpation is painful only after listening
  3. Palpation can change bowel sounds
  4. Bowel sounds disappear after inspection
Show answer

C. Palpation can change bowel sounds

The order for the abdomen is inspection, auscultation, percussion, then palpation, so touching does not alter what is heard.

2. A patient cannot close one eye or wrinkle the forehead on the same side, and the mouth droops. Why does this suggest Bell’s palsy rather than a stroke?

  1. Stroke always affects both sides of the face
  2. Forehead weakness points to a peripheral nerve
  3. Bell’s palsy never affects the mouth
  4. Stroke always causes eye closure weakness
Show answer

B. Forehead weakness points to a peripheral nerve

A central lesion such as a stroke usually spares the forehead because it receives input from both sides of the brain.

3. An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no distinct P waves. What is the main long-term risk of this rhythm?

  1. Episodes of low blood sugar
  2. Stroke from atrial clots
  3. Kidney stones
  4. Recurrent pneumonia
Show answer

B. Stroke from atrial clots

In atrial fibrillation, blood pools in the atria and can clot. Anticoagulation is considered based on stroke risk scores.
